title: Does deep alignment (Qi et al.'s objective) survive RLHF-style fine-tuning on benign data?

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Qi et al. (ICLR 2025) proposed deep alignment and showed it resists prefilling attacks. However, the specific question of whether deep alignment survives RLHF-style fine-tuning on benign data is partially addressed: Qi et al. showed benign fine-tuning degrades shallow alignment, and proposed a regularized fine-tuning objective. Multiple follow-up works (BOOSTER ICLR 2025, Antidote, SafeMERGE, SaLoRA ICLR 2025) study safety preservation during fine-tuning. The gap is measuring deep alignment specifically (via KL depth curves) through benign RLHF, which is a narrower replication-style experiment on an already well-studied problem.

title: Which layers encode the refusal decision? Locating alignment depth in activations, not just tokens

novelty_assessment.label: already_solved
novelty_assessment.reasoning: This idea is directly and comprehensively addressed by multiple published works. 'Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security' (ICLR 2025) localizes safety-critical layers. 'LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately' (Zhao et al.) shows harmfulness and refusal are orthogonal directions at specific layers. 'The Geometry of Refusal in Large Language Models: Concept Cones and Representational Independence' shows refusal signals concentrate in deeper layers and are multi-dimensional. 'Refusal Behavior in LLMs: A Nonlinear Perspective' (arXiv:2501.08145) identifies layer-specific refusal encoding. SafeSwitch (arXiv:2502.01042) steers behavior via internal activation signals at identified layers. The proposed probe-accuracy-vs-layer plot is a subset of these published findings.

title: Do adversarial suffixes (GCG) work by pushing refusal tokens to later positions or by suppressing them entirely?

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: The mechanism of GCG adversarial suffixes has been studied from multiple angles. Huang et al. (NAACL 2025) 'Stronger Universal and Transferable Attacks by Suppressing Refusals' explicitly targets refusal suppression in the optimization objective. Mask-GCG (arXiv:2509.06350) analyzes token importance within GCG suffixes. 'Beyond Suffixes: Token Position in GCG Adversarial Attacks' (arXiv:2602.03265) studies token positioning. However, the specific framing of 'delay vs suppress' as a binary classification of GCG mechanism, with per-token refusal probability distributions across positions, adds a systematic mechanistic analysis not directly performed in existing work. The suppression direction is known; the delay hypothesis and systematic comparison remain partially novel.

title: Does the 'Sure, here is' prefilling attack generalize to non-English refusal phrases?

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Prefilling attacks are well-documented (Anthropic prefill feature exploitation, AdaPPA arXiv:2409.07503, Prefill-level Jailbreak arXiv:2504.21038). Multilingual jailbreak vulnerability is also studied ('Automated Generation of Multilingual Jailbreak Prompts'). However, the specific intersection — testing whether prefilling with language-appropriate compliance phrases (not just English 'Sure, here is') affects alignment depth differently across languages — is not directly addressed. The combination of prefilling-specific methodology with cross-lingual alignment depth measurement (KL divergence per language) represents a mostly novel contribution.

title: How robust are linear-probe jailbreak detectors to simple paraphrasing and synonym substitution?

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: The robustness of probe-based jailbreak detectors to perturbations has been partially studied. 'What Features in Prompts Jailbreak LLMs?' (BlackboxNLP 2025) showed linear probes have limited cross-attack generalization. PromptScreen (arXiv:2512.19011) evaluated word-level models against paraphrasing and found early saturation and robustness limitations. SemanticSmooth uses paraphrasing defensively. However, the specific experiment — training a linear probe on activation representations and systematically measuring recall drop under controlled paraphrasing perturbation levels with a robustness curve — is a focused contribution not directly replicated. The general finding (probes struggle with perturbations) is known; the systematic quantification is partially novel.

title: Does the layer at which you extract activations for jailbreak detection matter for robustness?

novelty_assessment.label: largely_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: This question has been substantially addressed. 'Do Internal Layers of LLMs Reveal Patterns for Jailbreak Detection?' (arXiv:2510.06594) directly investigates layer-wise behavior for jailbreak detection. Alert (arXiv:2601.03600) identifies safety-relevant layers and selects discriminative modules, finding middle-to-late layers (12-26) are best. JBShield (USENIX Security 2025) computes embeddings at identified critical layers. The general finding — layer selection matters and middle-to-late layers are optimal — is well-established. The proposed heatmap of layer x attack-type AUROC is a specific visualization but the underlying findings are largely known.

title: Can a linear probe trained on one jailbreak category generalize to unseen categories?

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Cross-category generalization of jailbreak probes has been partially studied. 'What Features in Prompts Jailbreak LLMs?' (BlackboxNLP 2025) found linear and non-linear probes have limited ability to classify held-out attack methods. JBShield demonstrated strong transferability across unseen jailbreaks with only 30 calibration samples. However, the specific leave-one-category-out cross-validation design using StrongReject's 6 harm categories with AUROC per fold and comparison to baselines is a focused systematic evaluation not directly replicated. The general finding (poor linear probe generalization) is known; the proposed systematic StrongReject-based evaluation adds incremental value.

title: Is alignment depth correlated with model size within a single model family?

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: While scaling patterns in adversarial alignment have been studied (arXiv:2511.13788 found correlation between attacker size and harm), and alignment depth theory exists (Markov chain perspective, arXiv:2502.00669), the specific question of whether alignment depth (KL divergence metric from Qi et al.) scales with model size within a single family has not been directly investigated. Existing work focuses on adversarial robustness scaling or theoretical depth analysis, not empirical depth measurement across size variants. The proposed scatter plot of depth vs log(parameters) within one family is a clean, novel empirical contribution.

title: Do activation-based jailbreak detectors flag the same prompts that human red-teamers flag?

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Human vs. automated red teaming has been compared at a high level (multi-turn human jailbreaks study, Haize Labs x Goodfire mechanistic red teaming). However, the specific comparison of activation-based probe outputs to human red-teamer judgments using Cohen's kappa agreement statistics has not been published. Existing work either uses human red-teamers OR activation probes, but does not directly measure their agreement on the same prompt set. The qualitative analysis of disagreement cases (what probes miss vs. what humans miss) is a novel framing with deployment-relevant insights.

title: Can alignment depth be increased post-hoc by fine-tuning on safety-recovery examples, without touching the base training?

novelty_assessment.label: largely_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: This idea is largely addressed by existing work. Qi et al. (ICLR 2025) already proposed and demonstrated data augmentation with safety-recovery examples that 'deepens' safety alignment beyond initial tokens. Their augmented fine-tuning pushes KL divergence on later tokens of harmful responses to much higher levels. Multiple post-hoc safety recovery methods exist: SafeLoRA projects LoRA updates onto safety subspaces, RESTA negatively merges harmful task vectors, SafeMERGE uses selective layer-wise merging, and a dedicated ACL 2025 paper 'A Post-Hoc Approach to Safety Re-Alignment for Fine-Tuned LLMs' directly addresses this. The proposed experiment is essentially a replication of Qi et al.'s augmentation approach.

title: Do activation probes for jailbreak detection transfer across model families without retraining?

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Cross-model transfer of jailbreak-related representations has been studied. 'Jailbreak Transferability Emerges from Shared Representations' (arXiv:2506.12913) found that representational similarity predicts jailbreak transfer across 20 models. Non-linear MLP probes transfer better than linear probes to unseen layers. JBShield demonstrated transferability with minimal calibration. However, the specific experiment of training a linear probe on model A's activations and directly testing on model B's activations (3x3 transfer matrix with PCA projection) has not been systematically published. The representational basis for transfer is known; the specific cross-family probe transfer experiment is partially novel.

title: Is the 'safety-recovery' mechanism in deep alignment models visible in the attention patterns on harmful prefix tokens?

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel

title: How many labeled jailbreak examples are needed to train a reliable linear probe detector?

novelty_assessment.label: mostly_novel
novelty_assessment.reasoning: While linear probes for jailbreak detection have been studied (EMNLP 2025 Findings, BlackboxNLP 2025), and sample efficiency is discussed tangentially (JBShield needs only 30 calibration samples), no published work systematically constructs a learning curve showing AUROC vs training set size for activation-based linear probe jailbreak detectors. The data efficiency question is practical and deployment-critical. PromptScreen evaluated TF-IDF classifiers but not activation-based probes. The proposed 6-point learning curve with confidence intervals from 5 seeds is a clean experiment not directly available in the literature.

title: Does shallow alignment depth predict vulnerability to decoding parameter attacks (temperature/top-p manipulation)?

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: Qi et al. (ICLR 2025) already identified decoding parameter attacks as one manifestation of shallow alignment vulnerability and showed that their deep alignment augmentation reduced decoding exploits from 84.3% to 1.0% ASR. The proposed Spearman correlation across 5-6 models adds an empirical quantification not present in Qi et al., who focused on one model's before/after comparison. title: Do activation-based detectors degrade on 'low-perplexity' natural-language jailbreaks vs. GCG adversarial suffixes?

novelty_assessment.label: partially_addressed
novelty_assessment.reasoning: The distinction between GCG-style and natural-language jailbreaks for detection is partially explored. Perplexity filters trivially detect GCG suffixes but miss natural-language attacks. 'What Features in Prompts Jailbreak LLMs?' found that probes fail to generalize across held-out attack methods. PromptScreen noted word-level models saturate against paraphrasing. However, the specific controlled comparison of activation-based probe AUROC on balanced sets of GCG vs. natural-language jailbreaks with per-category confusion analysis has not been directly published. The general finding (type-specific blind spots exist) is known; the systematic head-to-head comparison adds moderate novelty.
